parts.context: Two employees at a community pharmacy are dealing with a problem before a vaccination clinic.

lines: Bronwyn, sorry to grab you before you’ve even got your coat off, but we’ve got a problem with the vaccine fridge. The alarm log says the temperature went up to eleven degrees at about two this morning.
Eleven? It’s supposed to stay between two and eight. For how long?
Almost four hours, according to the data logger. It looks like the power to that outlet tripped, and the fridge’s backup battery only lasted so long. Everything came back on by itself around six.

Right. Well, we can’t just assume the vaccines are fine. Anything that’s been outside the range has to be quarantined and reported to public health. They decide whether it can still be used. How many doses are in there?
About two hundred flu shots, and around forty doses of the shingles vaccine. And our Saturday flu clinic has a hundred and fifty people booked.
Of course it does. Did you call public health already?
I called the after-hours line at seven. They said they’ll review the logger data within two business days, and in the meantime we’re not to touch anything.
Two business days from today is Monday. So even if they clear the doses, it’s too late for Saturday. And I’m not about to give anyone a vaccine that might not work, just to keep the schedule.
Agreed. So what do we do with a hundred and fifty appointments?

Let’s think it through. First thing, label everything in that fridge ‘Do not use’ and move it all into the backup fridge in the office, so it’s at least back in range while we wait. Then we can talk about Saturday.
I’ll do that right now. The backup fridge has room if I take out the staff lunches.

qs.q: What happened to the vaccine fridge?
o: Its alarm stopped working at two in the morning.
It was too warm inside for several hours overnight.
Its backup battery was removed by mistake.
It was without power for two business days.
qs.ev: Almost four hours, according to the data logger.
qs.x: The temperature rose to eleven degrees, above the safe range, for almost four hours. “Two business days” is how long public health needs to review the data, not how long the power was off.

qs.q: What must happen to the affected vaccines?
o: They must be thrown out immediately.
They must be used up before Monday.
They must be returned to the supplier.
They must be set aside until an agency decides.
qs.ev: Anything that’s been outside the range has to be quarantined and reported to public health.
qs.x: The doses are quarantined and public health decides whether they can be used. Nobody says to throw them out; Monday is simply when the decision is expected.

qs.q: Why does Bronwyn rule out using the original doses on Saturday?
o: A decision about them will not come in time.
Public health has already said they are unsafe.
There are not enough doses for every appointment.
The doses are needed for the shingles clinic.
qs.ev: So even if they clear the doses, it’s too late for Saturday.
qs.x: The review will finish on Monday at the earliest, after the Saturday clinic. Public health has not said the doses are unsafe – it has not decided yet.

lines: Could we just order new stock? The distributor usually delivers in two days.
Usually. But flu vaccine is allocated by public health, not ordered like shampoo. I checked the portal on my phone on the way in. Our next allocation isn’t until the twentieth.
What about borrowing from another pharmacy? Westgate Drugs is only five minutes away.
We’re not allowed to transfer publicly funded vaccine between pharmacies without public health approval. And honestly, I called Westgate’s manager on my way in, and they’re short as well.
Okay. Then do we just postpone the clinic a week and call all hundred and fifty people?
That’s what I’m trying to avoid. A lot of those bookings are seniors who arranged rides with family. Some of them booked months ago. If we push it, I’d bet a third of them won’t rebook at all.
What about running Saturday with fewer people? There are some doses in the backup fridge that we never moved, right? Those were never in the bad fridge.
Thirty doses, maybe. Better than nothing, but that still leaves a hundred and twenty people to call.
Hmm. Hang on – doesn’t the public health unit run its own flu clinics at the Lakeshore Community Centre on weekends? Maybe they’d take some of our people.
They do, but they book through their own system. Our patients would have to start from scratch, and those spots fill up fast.
Unless we ask them directly. My cousin Aiko coordinates their clinics. I could at least give her a call.
It’s worth a try. Go ahead, and let me know what she says.

qs.q: Why can’t the pharmacy simply order new flu vaccine?
o: The distributor needs two days to deliver it.
The pharmacy’s online ordering portal is down.
Supplies are handed out by an outside authority.
The pharmacy has spent its annual budget.
qs.ev: flu vaccine is allocated by public health, not ordered like shampoo
qs.x: Public health allocates flu vaccine, and the next allocation is on the twentieth. The two-day delivery applies to normal stock, which flu vaccine is not; the portal was working when she checked it.

qs.q: What is Bronwyn’s main concern about postponing the clinic?
o: Many patients might not come back at all.
Seniors would have to pay for a second ride.
Calling every patient would take a full week.
Westgate Drugs would take their patients.
qs.ev: If we push it, I’d bet a third of them won’t rebook at all.
qs.x: She predicts a third of patients would never rebook, so they would miss their flu shots. Rides are mentioned to explain why moving dates is hard, not because of cost.

qs.q: What is Bronwyn’s opinion of running Saturday with only the doses from the backup fridge?
o: It would solve the problem completely.
It would break public health rules.
It is too risky to attempt at all.
It would help a little but not enough.
qs.ev: Better than nothing, but that still leaves a hundred and twenty people to call.
qs.x: “Better than nothing, but…” shows limited approval: thirty doses still leave 120 people without appointments. Those doses were never in the bad fridge, so there is no rule problem.

lines: Okay, I talked to Aiko. Public health can’t move any of our patients into their own clinics, but she had a different idea.
Because our doses are already quarantined, she can ask the vaccine team to fast-track the review. If the logger data looks okay, they might give us an answer by Friday at noon instead of Monday.
Friday at noon. That’s cutting it close, but it’s possible. And if they don’t clear them?
Then she said she could release a small emergency supply, sixty doses, which we could pick up from their office on Friday afternoon. Add our thirty, and that’s ninety.
So in the worst case, we can vaccinate ninety people and we need to move sixty.
Right. I was thinking I could start calling the sixty youngest, healthiest people on the list this afternoon and offer them next Saturday instead, since they’re the lowest risk.

The people who booked online tend to be younger, so that list should be easy enough to pull. But don’t call anyone yet. If the doses are cleared on Friday, we won’t need to move anybody, and I don’t want to confuse people by calling them twice.
But if we wait until Friday afternoon, that’s not much notice for them.

Fair point. Let’s compromise. Draft the message today, and we’ll send it at noon on Friday, the moment we hear either way. Meanwhile, I’ll email the district manager about getting an electrician to look at that outlet.
Sounds good. I’ll put the message together this morning.

qs.q: What did Aiko offer to do?
o: Move some patients into public health clinics
Ask for a quicker decision about the doses
Deliver sixty doses on Saturday morning
Check the fridge’s data logger herself
qs.ev: she can ask the vaccine team to fast-track the review
qs.x: Aiko can ask for the review to be fast-tracked, possibly by Friday noon. Public health specifically cannot take the pharmacy’s patients, and the emergency doses would be picked up Friday afternoon, not delivered Saturday.

qs.q: What will Kenji most likely do this morning?
o: Phone the sixty youngest patients on the list
Collect the emergency doses from public health
Prepare a message that will be sent later
Arrange for an electrician to inspect the outlet
qs.ev: Draft the message today, and we’ll send it at noon on Friday
qs.x: Bronwyn tells him not to call anyone yet but to draft a message for Friday noon, and he agrees. Contacting the district manager about an electrician is Bronwyn’s job.

parts.context: A father is calling a youth counselling centre about his son.

lines: Northside Youth Counselling, this is Marisol. How can I help?

Hi, my name’s Gareth. I’m calling about my son, Felix. He’s sixteen, and he’s been having a really hard time since we moved here in August. He’s not sleeping, he’s skipping classes, and he barely talks to us. His school counsellor suggested I get in touch with you.

I’m sorry to hear that. I can certainly explain how it works. One thing to know first: at sixteen, Felix can consent to counselling on his own, so ideally he would be the one to contact us, or at least be part of the call. We find young people do much better when it’s their own choice.
I was afraid you’d say that. He’s sort of agreed to talk to someone, but he said he won’t call a stranger on the phone.
That’s really common. He can also fill out the intake form online or send us a text. A lot of teens prefer that. Do you think he’d do that?
Text? Probably, yes. He texts a lot more than he talks.

Then that’s the easiest route. Once we have his form, a counsellor will contact him within five business days to book a first session. Our sessions are free for anyone under twenty-five, and they can be in person, by video or by phone.
Free? That’s a relief. I was looking at private therapists, and they were charging a hundred and sixty dollars an hour.

No cost at all; we’re funded by the province. The only catch is that the wait for regular weekly counselling is about six weeks right now. But we also have a drop-in session every Wednesday from three to seven, with no appointment needed, so he could be seen in the meantime.
Wednesday after school would work. Can I go in with him?

You can certainly come along and wait, and some teens like having a parent in the room for the first few minutes. But it’s Felix’s decision. And I should mention that what he says in his sessions is confidential, so the counsellor won’t share details with you unless there’s a safety concern.
I suppose that’s fair. I just want to know he’s okay.
That’s completely understandable. We also run a free four-week evening group for parents of teenagers, which a lot of parents find helpful. The next one starts in January.
Maybe. Let me get Felix sorted first. Could you text me the link to the form, and I’ll forward it to him?
Of course. I’ll send it right now.

qs.q: Why does Marisol suggest that Felix contact the centre himself?
o: He is old enough to agree to counselling himself.
Parents are not permitted to call the centre.
The school counsellor has already referred him.
The intake form must be signed by the teen.
qs.ev: at sixteen, Felix can consent to counselling on his own
qs.x: At sixteen he can give his own consent, and teens do better when it is their choice. Parents can call – Marisol is talking to Gareth – so the second option is wrong.

qs.q: How does Gareth feel when Marisol says Felix should be the one to contact them?
o: Relieved that he doesn’t need to be involved
Annoyed that the centre’s rules are so strict
Doubtful that his son will be willing to phone
Confident that his son will call that day
qs.ev: he said he won’t call a stranger on the phone
qs.x: “I was afraid you’d say that” and Felix refusing to call a stranger show Gareth doubts his son will phone. He is worried, not annoyed with the centre.

qs.q: What does Gareth learn about the cost of counselling?
o: Sessions cost one hundred sixty dollars an hour.
Felix will not have to pay anything.
The province pays for the first six weeks.
Video sessions cost less than in-person ones.
qs.ev: Our sessions are free for anyone under twenty-five
qs.x: Sessions are free for anyone under twenty-five. $160 an hour is what private therapists charge, and six weeks is the waiting time, not a funding limit.

qs.q: Why does Marisol mention the Wednesday drop-in session?
o: It is the only time Felix can see a counsellor.
Parents are required to attend it first.
It replaces the online intake form.
It offers help before weekly sessions begin.
qs.ev: so he could be seen in the meantime
qs.x: The drop-in lets Felix get support during the six-week wait for regular counselling. It does not replace the intake form, and parents are not required to attend.

qs.q: What does Gareth reluctantly accept?
o: That the parents’ group is already full
That he won’t hear what his son discusses
That Felix must go to sessions alone
That the wait could be longer than six weeks
qs.ev: I suppose that’s fair.
qs.x: “I suppose that’s fair” responds to the confidentiality rule, showing reluctant acceptance that he won’t hear details. Felix may bring a parent into the room if he wants, so he need not go alone.

parts.context: A new member is attending an orientation at a community fitness centre.

lines: Okay, Anjali, welcome to Brookfield Community Fitness. This orientation usually takes about twenty minutes. Did you sign up for the regular membership or the off-peak one?
The regular one, monthly. Forty-nine dollars, I think? Although, honestly, I mostly come in the middle of the day, because I work evenings.

Oh, then you might want to switch. The off-peak membership is thirty-five dollars a month, and it covers weekdays from ten to four, plus anytime on weekends. If that matches your schedule, there’s no reason to pay for the full one. You can switch at the front desk, and there’s no fee for changing within your first week.
Really? Great. I’ll do that on my way out.

Now, group classes. You book them through our app, up to seven days ahead. Spots go fast, especially for the noon spin class and Saturday yoga. If you can’t make it, cancel at least two hours before the class, or there’s a five-dollar no-show fee. And if you miss three classes in one month without cancelling, your booking privileges are suspended for two weeks.
Two weeks! Okay, I’ll be careful. Can I bring a friend sometimes?

Yes, you get two free guest passes a month. Guests have to be at least sixteen and sign a waiver at the desk. One thing, though: off-peak members can only use guest passes during their own hours, so not on weekday evenings.
That’s fine. My sister would come on weekends anyway. What about the pool? I have a nine-year-old son.

Children under twelve need an adult in the water with them, not just on the deck. Family swim is Saturday and Sunday from one to three. Kids don’t need a membership for family swim, but there’s a four-dollar drop-in fee each time.
Day lockers are free; just bring your own lock. But don’t leave anything overnight. Staff cut any locks that are still on at closing, and the contents go to lost and found.
Good to know. Oh, and my physiotherapist said I should try a few sessions with a trainer because of my shoulder. Is that extra?

Your first personal training session is free, and after that it’s sixty dollars an hour, or two hundred and fifty for five. Since you mentioned your shoulder, I’d recommend booking with Carla. She has a kinesiology background, and she works a lot with injuries.
Perfect. Last question. I’m going to India for two months in March. Do I have to keep paying the whole time?
No, you can freeze your membership for up to three months a year. It’s ten dollars a month while it’s frozen, and you just need to request it at least a week ahead.
That’s much better than paying full price. Thanks, Tobias, this has been really helpful.

qs.q: Why does Tobias suggest that Anjali change her membership?
o: The regular membership is being discontinued.
She is paying for hours that she doesn’t use.
Off-peak members receive extra guest passes.
There will be a fee if she changes after today.
qs.ev: If that matches your schedule, there’s no reason to pay for the full one.
qs.x: She comes midday, so she is paying for evening access she doesn’t need. There is no fee for switching within the first week, not just today.

qs.q: What happens if a member misses three booked classes in a month without cancelling?
o: Their membership is suspended for two weeks.
They must pay an extra ten-dollar fee.
They lose their guest passes that month.
They temporarily cannot reserve classes.
qs.ev: your booking privileges are suspended for two weeks
qs.x: Only booking privileges are suspended, so they cannot reserve classes for two weeks. The membership itself is not suspended – that option is the trap.

qs.q: When could Anjali’s sister use a guest pass with her, if Anjali switches to off-peak?
o: Saturday at 7 p.m.
Wednesday at 6 p.m.
Monday at 8 a.m.
Friday at 5 p.m.
qs.ev: it covers weekdays from ten to four, plus anytime on weekends
qs.x: Off-peak guests can come only during off-peak hours: weekdays 10–4 or anytime on weekends. Saturday evening qualifies; the weekday times are all outside 10–4.

qs.q: What is required for Anjali’s son to use the pool?
o: He must have his own membership.
He must be at least twelve years old.
His mother must swim alongside him.
He must sign a waiver at the desk.
qs.ev: Children under twelve need an adult in the water with them, not just on the deck.
qs.x: Because he is under twelve, an adult must be in the water with him. Kids don’t need a membership for family swim; waivers are for guests.

qs.q: Why does Tobias recommend Carla?
o: She offers the cheapest training packages.
Her experience suits someone with an injury.
She is the only trainer free at midday.
She gives clients a free first session.
qs.ev: she works a lot with injuries
qs.x: Carla has a kinesiology background and works with injuries, which fits Anjali’s shoulder. The free first session applies to all trainers, so it is not a reason to choose Carla.

qs.q: How much will Anjali pay for the two months she is away?
o: Twenty dollars in total
Seventy dollars in total
Ten dollars in total
Thirty-five dollars in total
qs.ev: It’s ten dollars a month while it’s frozen
qs.x: A frozen membership costs $10 a month, so two months cost $20. Seventy dollars would be two months of the off-peak fee without a freeze.

parts.context: You will hear a news report about a hospital in a small town.

lines: The emergency department at Pine Hollow District Hospital will close overnight on at least six nights in December because of a shortage of nurses, the regional health network confirmed today. The department will shut its doors from seven p.m. to seven a.m. on the affected nights, which will be posted on the hospital’s website and social media at least forty-eight hours in advance. During closures, residents are being told to call 911 in an emergency. Paramedics will take patients to Crestview General, about fifty-five kilometres away. The network says the closures are a last resort. It has been relying on agency nurses, who are flown in from other provinces, but it says it couldn’t fill enough shifts over the holidays. The hospital currently has nine vacant full-time nursing positions out of twenty-four. Pine Hollow’s mayor, Wendell Briggs, says the town has heard these promises before.

This is the third winter in a row. Every time, we’re told it’s temporary, and every time, it gets a little worse. What worries me most isn’t the heart attacks. People know to call 911 for those. It’s the parent with a feverish baby at two in the morning, sitting at the kitchen table, wondering whether it’s serious enough to drive an hour on winter roads.

To help with that, the network is extending the hours of its free nurse advice line, which will now be staffed by a nurse around the clock instead of until midnight. It is also offering signing bonuses of up to twenty thousand dollars to nurses who commit to working at the hospital for two years, and says three nurses have already accepted offers to start in the new year. The mayor says town council will vote next week on a proposal to offer incoming health workers a year of free rent in town-owned housing. Critics, including the provincial nurses’ union, argue that bonuses and housing perks only shift nurses from one community to another, and say the real problem is workload. The union is calling for minimum nurse-to-patient ratios across the province.

qs.q: What will happen at the hospital on certain nights in December?
o: Only patients arriving by ambulance will be treated.
Agency nurses will run the emergency department.
Emergency care there will be unavailable overnight.
The department will close without any notice.
qs.ev: The department will shut its doors from seven p.m. to seven a.m. on the affected nights
qs.x: The emergency department will close from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. on those nights. Closures are posted at least 48 hours ahead, and ambulance patients go to Crestview, not Pine Hollow.

qs.q: According to the report, why are the closures happening?
o: Too few nursing shifts could be covered.
Agency nurses refused to travel in winter.
Crestview General asked for more nurses.
Nine nurses resigned in the past month.
qs.ev: it couldn’t fill enough shifts over the holidays
qs.x: The network could not fill enough shifts, even with agency nurses. The nine vacancies are open positions; nobody says nine nurses recently resigned.

qs.q: What is the mayor’s greatest worry?
o: People will not call 911 for heart attacks.
Paramedics will be unable to reach Crestview.
The network will close the department for good.
Residents won’t know when to seek urgent care.
qs.ev: It’s the parent with a feverish baby at two in the morning
qs.x: He fears people facing uncertain situations, like a feverish baby, won’t know if it is serious enough to travel. He says people DO know to call 911 for heart attacks.

qs.q: What change is being made to the nurse advice line?
o: It will be free for the first time.
It will be available at all hours.
It will close at midnight on weekends.
It will be answered by paramedics.
qs.ev: will now be staffed by a nurse around the clock instead of until midnight
qs.x: The line will run around the clock instead of closing at midnight. It was already free, and it is staffed by nurses, not paramedics.

qs.q: What is the union’s view of the bonuses and housing offers?
o: They should be offered across the province.
They are too small to attract any nurses.
They move the shortage rather than solve it.
They should be paid for by the town.
qs.ev: bonuses and housing perks only shift nurses from one community to another
qs.x: The union says perks just move nurses between communities while the real issue, workload, remains. It wants province-wide staffing ratios, not province-wide bonuses.

parts.context: Three staff members at a long-term care home are discussing a problem with a visiting therapy dog program.

lines: Thanks for coming, both of you. As you know, the family of Mr. Delgado on the second floor has filed a formal complaint about the therapy dog visits. He’s quite allergic, and last Thursday he had a bad reaction after the dog had been in the lounge.
A bad reaction is putting it mildly. His eyes were swollen almost shut, and we had to call the physician. He was fine by the evening, but it was frightening for him.
And the family’s position is pretty firm. They want the dog program stopped. His daughter told me her father didn’t choose to live with a dog, and that this is his home, not a petting zoo.

I understand how they feel, I really do. But this program is the single most popular thing we offer. Thirty-eight residents signed up. For some of our residents with advanced dementia, it’s the only time all week they really light up.
No one’s disputing that. But we have a duty of care to every resident, not just the majority. If one person gets hurt, the popularity of the program doesn’t really matter.
Could we keep the dog on the third floor only? Mr. Delgado almost never goes up there.

The problem is the dander. It travels on clothing and through the ventilation. Our building shares one air system between the second and third floors. Keeping the dog upstairs would reduce his exposure, but it wouldn’t eliminate it.
What about the ground floor, then? The activity room has its own entrance from the garden, and I’m fairly sure it got a separate air system during the renovation.
If that’s true, it changes things. I’d want maintenance to confirm it in writing, though.
There’s still the issue of residents who can’t easily get downstairs. Some of the people who benefit most are in wheelchairs or need two staff to transfer.
We could book porters for visit days. It’s only two hours every second Thursday. That’s manageable.
Maybe. But staffing on Thursdays is already thin. I’m not going to pull care aides off the floor to move people to a dog visit. If recreation can cover it with volunteers, fine.
I think I can find volunteers. The high school co-op students are looking for placements.
Here’s my worry, though. Even if we move the program, the family wants it stopped. If we just tell them it’s moving downstairs, they might take this to the ministry.
Do you really think they’d do that?
Honestly, I think they’re more upset about how it was handled than about the dog itself. No one called them the day it happened. They found out when they visited on Saturday.
That’s on us. The incident report was filed, but the call to the family got missed during shift change.
Then I think we need to start there. Apologize properly first, and then show them the plan.
I’d also suggest offering them a meeting with the dog’s handler, so they can ask questions. And we should put a sign on the activity room door on visit days.
And I want a note in Mr. Delgado’s care plan that he isn’t brought to the ground floor on dog days. Plus, the handler should use a lint roller and change jackets before leaving the activity room.
Fine by me. So, we pause the visits for now, maintenance confirms the air system, and if it’s separate, we restart in the activity room with volunteers handling transfers.
And I’ll call the family this afternoon to apologize and set up a meeting.
Good. But if maintenance says the air is shared, we’ll have to look for another option entirely.
Agreed. Let’s meet again once we hear back from maintenance.

qs.q: What does Mr. Delgado’s family want?
o: An end to the dog visits
The dog kept off the second floor
Their father moved to another room
A meeting with the dog’s handler
qs.ev: They want the dog program stopped.
qs.x: The family wants the program stopped entirely. Keeping the dog off certain floors and meeting the handler are staff ideas, not the family’s demands.

qs.q: What is Rosalind’s main argument for keeping the program?
o: The family had agreed to it in advance.
The dog has never caused a reaction before.
It brings rare joy to some residents.
It is cheaper than other activities.
qs.ev: it’s the only time all week they really light up
qs.x: She stresses that for some residents with dementia, the visits are the only time they light up all week. Cost and earlier consent are never mentioned.

qs.q: What is Sunita’s attitude toward the program’s popularity?
o: She thinks it has been exaggerated.
She believes it should settle the issue.
She is pleased that more residents joined.
She considers it less important than safety.
qs.ev: If one person gets hurt, the popularity of the program doesn’t really matter.
qs.x: She accepts it is popular (“no one’s disputing that”) but says the duty of care to every resident comes first. She does not doubt the numbers.

qs.q: Why does Sunita reject keeping the dog on the third floor?
o: Mr. Delgado often visits that floor.
Allergens could still reach him through the air.
The third floor has no room for the visits.
Other residents upstairs are also allergic.
qs.ev: Our building shares one air system between the second and third floors.
qs.x: Dander travels through the shared ventilation, so exposure would only be reduced. Emeka says Mr. Delgado almost never goes upstairs, so the first option is wrong.

qs.q: What condition does Sunita set on using the activity room?
o: Its ventilation must be officially confirmed.
It must have a separate garden entrance.
It must be renovated before visits restart.
It may only be used by residents who walk.
qs.ev: I’d want maintenance to confirm it in writing, though.
qs.x: She wants written confirmation from maintenance that the room has a separate air system. The garden entrance already exists and is not her condition.

qs.q: How does Sunita respond to the idea of booking porters?
o: She agrees if it happens only once a month.
She suggests the family pay for extra staff.
She offers to change the Thursday schedule.
She refuses to let it take aides from residents.
qs.ev: I’m not going to pull care aides off the floor to move people to a dog visit.
qs.x: She refuses to use care aides because Thursday staffing is thin, accepting only volunteers. She does not offer to change any schedule.

qs.q: What does Emeka think is really upsetting the family?
o: The dog visits happen too often.
Their father’s room is near the lounge.
They were not told promptly about the incident.
The program began without their consent.
qs.ev: No one called them the day it happened.
qs.x: He believes they are more upset about how it was handled: nobody called them, and they found out days later. Consent to the program is never raised.

qs.q: What have they decided to do first?
o: Restart the visits in the activity room next Thursday
Stop the visits until the air system is checked
Ask the ministry to review the family’s complaint
Replace the dog with a breed that sheds less
qs.ev: we pause the visits for now, maintenance confirms the air system
qs.x: Visits are paused until maintenance confirms the ventilation; only then will they restart downstairs. The ministry is what Emeka fears the family might contact, not a staff plan.

parts.context: You will hear a radio report about virtual medical clinics.

lines: It’s eleven o’clock on a Tuesday night, and Kayla Brennan’s four-year-old has a cough that won’t quit. A few years ago, Kayla would have waited until morning and spent half a day at a walk-in clinic. Instead, she opens an app on her phone, answers a few questions, and twenty minutes later she’s talking to a doctor by video. The doctor listens to the cough, asks her to hold the phone close to her daughter’s throat, and sends a prescription to the pharmacy for the morning. Kayla describes it as a lifesaver. She’s one of hundreds of thousands of Canadians using virtual-only clinics, services that offer appointments by phone or video and nothing else. For people without a family doctor, and there are millions of them, these clinics can feel like the only door that’s open. Supporters argue they also take pressure off emergency rooms and save patients time off work and travel costs, especially in rural areas. But many family physicians are uneasy. Dr. Ingrid Solberg has practised family medicine for twenty years.

I use video visits myself, and for some things they’re excellent – a medication review, test results, a follow-up for anxiety. My concern isn’t the technology. It’s when a stranger who has never seen you before, and will never see you again, is making decisions without your history. I had a patient who used a virtual clinic four times in one year for headaches. Four different doctors, four different prescriptions. Nobody connected the dots. When she finally came to see me in person, her blood pressure was dangerously high.

Researchers have also raised concerns about follow-up. A recent provincial review found that patients of virtual-only clinics were somewhat more likely to end up in an emergency department within a week of their appointment than patients seen in person, though the authors note that the two groups may not be directly comparable. There’s also a debate about money. In several provinces, virtual clinics bill the public system at the same rate as in-person visits, even though their costs are lower. Some family doctors argue that this draws physicians away from comprehensive practices into easier, better-paid work. Virtual clinic operators reject that. They point out that many of their doctors work part-time on the platforms in addition to running in-person practices, and that some are semi-retired physicians who would otherwise have left medicine altogether. Several provinces are now considering rules that would require virtual clinics to send visit notes to a patient’s family doctor, where one exists, and to refer patients to in-person care for certain conditions. Dr. Solberg supports those rules, but says they don’t go far enough.
Sending notes to a family doctor is lovely in theory. But the people relying most on these clinics are precisely the ones who don’t have a family doctor. So the notes go nowhere.
For her part, Kayla says she’d take a family doctor in a heartbeat. She’s been on the waiting list for three years.

qs.q: Why does the reporter begin with Kayla’s story?
o: To show that virtual clinics prescribe too quickly
To show the convenience that attracts many users
To explain how parents should treat a cough
To criticize walk-in clinics for long waits
qs.ev: Kayla describes it as a lifesaver.
qs.x: Her late-night video visit illustrates why people find virtual clinics so convenient. The walk-in clinic is mentioned only as what she used to do, not as the target of criticism.

qs.q: What is Dr. Solberg’s main concern about virtual-only clinics?
o: Video quality is too poor for most diagnoses.
Doctors there refuse to review medications.
Patients use them mainly for minor illnesses.
Doctors there lack the patient’s history.
qs.ev: making decisions without your history
qs.x: Her concern is strangers deciding without knowing a patient’s history. She says the technology is not the problem and even calls video good for medication reviews.

qs.q: What does the story of the patient with headaches illustrate?
o: Fragmented care hid a serious problem.
Virtual doctors prescribe stronger drugs.
Headaches are hard to diagnose by video.
The patient refused to see her own doctor.
qs.ev: Nobody connected the dots.
qs.x: Four different doctors never linked the visits, so dangerously high blood pressure went unnoticed. The issue was lack of continuity, not the video format itself.

qs.q: What does the report say about the provincial review?
o: It proved virtual care causes more emergency visits.
It found no difference between the two groups.
Its comparison may not be entirely fair.
It was carried out by virtual clinic operators.
qs.ev: the authors note that the two groups may not be directly comparable
qs.x: The authors themselves warn the groups may not be comparable, so the result is not proof. It did find a difference – virtual patients were somewhat more likely to visit emergency.

qs.q: How do virtual clinic operators respond to criticism about doctors?
o: They admit that their doctors are paid more.
They say their platforms keep some doctors working.
They say most of their doctors work online full-time.
They plan to stop billing the public system.
qs.ev: some are semi-retired physicians who would otherwise have left medicine altogether
qs.x: Operators argue many doctors work part-time online and some semi-retired doctors would otherwise have quit, so the platforms keep them practising. They say part-time, not full-time.

qs.q: Why does Dr. Solberg think the proposed rules are not enough?
o: Many users have no doctor to receive the notes.
Family doctors don’t read notes from other clinics.
The rules won’t apply to rural patients.
In-person referrals take too long to arrange.
qs.ev: the people relying most on these clinics are precisely the ones who don’t have a family doctor
qs.x: Notes can only go to an existing family doctor, and the main users don’t have one, so “the notes go nowhere”. She doesn’t claim doctors ignore notes.

p1.meta: From: Callum Forsythe | To: Ines Forsythe | Subject: A strange few weeks (and a big ask)
p1.text:
Hi Ines,

Sorry I’ve been so quiet since New Year’s. It has been a strange few weeks. You probably heard from Mom that Priya broke her leg on our ski trip – but I suspect Mom made it sound much less dramatic than it was. It was a bad break in two places, and she had surgery the next morning. She’s home now, but she can’t put any weight on that leg for at least eight weeks, and the surgeon says it could be longer.

So I’ve suddenly become a full-time nurse, cook, chauffeur and referee, on top of my job. The twins think it’s all very exciting, especially the wheelchair, which they keep trying to borrow for races down the hallway. Priya is handling it better than I would. She’s working from the couch and has organized the whole house from there like an air traffic controller.

We have had help. The home-care program sends a personal support worker for two hours every weekday morning to help Priya shower and dress, which has been a lifesaver, although the schedule changes constantly and we never know exactly who is coming. Our neighbours also set up a meal train, so we’ve eaten more lasagna in three weeks than in the last three years. I’m not complaining – well, maybe a little.

The hard part is next month. My company has a client project in Winnipeg from February 10 to 16, and I’m the only one who knows the system well enough to lead it. I tried to get out of it, but my manager made it pretty clear that this one isn’t optional. Priya insists she’ll manage, but realistically she can’t get the twins to school and to hockey on crutches.

So here’s my big ask: could you come and stay with us that week? I know it means taking time off, and I’d pay for your flight, of course. You’d have the guest room, and the twins have already promised to behave, for whatever that’s worth.

No pressure – just let me know when you can.

Love,
Callum

qs.q: What does Callum suggest about the way their mother described Priya’s accident?
o: She exaggerated how bad the injury was.
She had not heard about the accident yet.
She played down how bad it was.
She blamed Priya for going skiing.
qs.ev: I suspect Mom made it sound much less dramatic than it was
qs.x: “Much less dramatic than it was” means Mom minimized the injury. The first option reverses this: she understated, not exaggerated, it.

qs.q: How is Priya coping with her injury?
o: She has had to stop working until spring.
She relies on the twins to run the household.
She is frustrated by the home-care schedule.
She is managing the household from her seat.
qs.ev: She’s working from the couch and has organized the whole house from there like an air traffic controller.
qs.x: She runs the household from the couch like an air traffic controller and is still working. It is Callum, not Priya, who mentions the changing home-care schedule.

qs.q: What does Callum say about the personal support worker?
o: The service is helpful but unpredictable.
The worker comes every day, including weekends.
The worker also prepares meals for the family.
The service costs more than they expected.
qs.ev: although the schedule changes constantly and we never know exactly who is coming
qs.x: He calls it a lifesaver but says the schedule keeps changing and they never know who will come. The worker comes on weekday mornings only, and meals come from neighbours.

qs.q: How does Callum feel about the meal train?
o: He would prefer that the neighbours stop.
He is embarrassed to accept so much help.
He thinks the meals are too expensive.
He is grateful but a bit tired of the food.
qs.ev: I’m not complaining – well, maybe a little.
qs.x: He appreciates the help but jokes that they have eaten far too much lasagna – “maybe a little” of a complaint. He never asks the neighbours to stop.

qs.q: Why can’t Callum stay home in February?
o: His manager has offered him a promotion.
His employer insists that he lead a project.
He must attend a training course in Winnipeg.
Priya has asked him to keep working.
qs.ev: my manager made it pretty clear that this one isn’t optional
qs.x: He is the only one who can lead the Winnipeg client project, and his manager says it isn’t optional. It is a client project, not a training course.

qs.q: What is Callum’s main reason for writing?
o: To ask Ines to drive Priya to appointments
To invite Ines to watch the twins’ hockey
To ask Ines to look after the children for a week
To tell Ines that Priya needs more surgery
qs.ev: could you come and stay with us that week?
qs.x: He asks Ines to stay during his trip because Priya can’t take the twins to school and hockey. Hockey is part of the childcare, not an invitation to watch.

reply.intro: Here is Ines’s response to Callum. Complete it by choosing the best option for each blank.
reply.text:
Hi Callum,

Poor Priya! Please tell her I’m sending hugs – and that she should keep the twins well away from that wheelchair. Honestly, I had no idea it was so serious. Mom only told me Priya had {1}.

Of course I’ll come. I checked with my supervisor this morning, and I can take the whole week. I’ll fly in on {2} so that we have an evening together before you leave for Winnipeg.

And please don’t pay for my flight. I have travel points I’ve been saving for ages, and you’ve got enough on your plate right now. If you really want to thank me, {3}.

One practical question: since the support worker only comes {4}, will Priya need help in the evenings, or is she fine once she’s dressed? Also, send me the twins’ schedule. I’m happy to {5}, although I warn you, I know nothing about hockey.

See you soon,
Ines

o: needed two operations
been told to rest for months
broken her leg in two places
taken a little tumble skiing
blanks.ev: I suspect Mom made it sound much less dramatic than it was
blanks.x: Ines didn’t realize it was serious because Mom described it lightly – “a little tumble”. Saying Priya broke her leg in two places would have made it sound serious.

o: the 10th
the 12th
the 9th
the 16th
blanks.x: Callum leaves on February 10, so arriving on the 9th gives them an evening together before he goes. The 10th would be too late.

o: pay for my flight home instead
save me a plate of that lasagna
let me use the wheelchair for races
stay in Winnipeg an extra day
blanks.ev: we’ve eaten more lasagna in three weeks than in the last three years
blanks.x: A playful thank-you that refers to the meal-train lasagna fits the friendly tone. Asking him to pay for a flight contradicts “please don’t pay for my flight”.

o: on weekday mornings
on weekends
in the evenings
every other day
blanks.x: The worker comes for two hours every weekday morning, which is why Ines asks about evenings. “In the evenings” contradicts her own question.

o: teach them how to ski
help Priya with her exercises
work from home that week
do the school runs and rink trips
blanks.ev: she can’t get the twins to school and to hockey on crutches
blanks.x: Callum’s worry is getting the twins to school and hockey, so Ines offers to drive them – hence her joke about knowing nothing about hockey.

p3.title: Turn It Down: Hearing Loss Is Getting Younger
paras: Audiologists across the country say they are seeing a change in who walks through their doors. Hearing loss was long considered a condition of old age, but clinics now report growing numbers of patients in their twenties and thirties complaining of muffled hearing or a constant ringing in their ears, known as tinnitus. At the Kestrel Bay Hearing Centre, audiologist Nadine Pruitt says roughly one in five new patients is under forty, compared with almost none when she started her career. Many of them, she says, are surprised to learn that the damage is permanent. “People assume hearing is like a sunburn – that it will recover,” she says. “After a concert, the ringing often fades, so they think everything is fine. But each time, some of the tiny hair cells in the inner ear may be lost for good.”

Personal audio devices are a major part of the problem, though not because they are inherently dangerous. Most earbuds can reach volumes above one hundred decibels, roughly as loud as a chainsaw, and many people turn the volume up to drown out noise on buses and subways. Safe listening depends on both volume and time: at eighty-five decibels, about the level of heavy traffic, damage can begin after eight hours, but every increase of three decibels cuts the safe time in half. Noise-cancelling headphones can help, researchers say, because listeners no longer need to compete with background sound. Many phones now include settings that warn users or limit volume automatically, but surveys suggest that most young people have never switched them on.

Loud venues add to the risk. Sound levels at concerts, clubs and even fitness classes regularly exceed one hundred decibels, and spin studios have attracted particular attention because instructors often turn the music up to motivate riders. Some cities in Europe require venues to display sound levels and offer free earplugs, but Canada has no national standard for public venues. Workplace noise is regulated, which means that the bartender at a nightclub is protected by occupational rules that do not apply to the customers standing a few metres away. Musicians, meanwhile, have become some of the most vocal advocates for hearing protection. Several well-known performers now wear custom earplugs on stage and openly encourage their fans to do the same, something that would have been unthinkable a generation ago.

Experts stress that protecting your hearing does not mean giving up music. Audiologists recommend the “60/60 rule”: listening at no more than sixty percent of maximum volume for no more than sixty minutes at a time. High-fidelity earplugs, which reduce volume evenly rather than muffling sound, cost between twenty and forty dollars and can make concerts more comfortable. Anyone who notices ringing that lasts more than a day, or who finds it hard to follow conversations in noisy rooms, should book a hearing test. In most provinces, a basic test by an audiologist is not covered by public health insurance, although many workplace benefit plans pay for it. Early detection matters, Pruitt says, because hearing aids work best when they are fitted before the brain has become used to silence.

qs.q: Some people wrongly believe their hearing will heal after exposure to loud noise.
qs.ev: People assume hearing is like a sunburn – that it will recover
qs.x: Paragraph A: people assume hearing recovers like a sunburn, but the damage may be permanent.

qs.q: How long someone listens matters as well as how loud the sound is.
qs.ev: Safe listening depends on both volume and time
qs.x: Paragraph B: safe listening depends on both volume and time, with safe time halving every three decibels.

qs.q: Employees at noisy venues have legal protections that customers do not.
qs.ev: the bartender at a nightclub is protected by occupational rules that do not apply to the customers standing a few metres away
qs.x: Paragraph C: workplace noise rules protect the bartender but not customers nearby.

qs.q: Young people who use noise-cancelling headphones have less hearing damage than those who use ordinary earbuds.
qs.x: Paragraph B says noise-cancelling headphones can help, but no comparison of hearing damage between users is reported.

qs.q: Some earplugs lower the volume without distorting the sound.
qs.ev: reduce volume evenly rather than muffling sound
qs.x: Paragraph D: high-fidelity earplugs reduce volume evenly instead of muffling sound.

qs.q: Exercise classes are among the places where loud music has caused concern.
qs.ev: spin studios have attracted particular attention
qs.x: Paragraph C: spin studios have attracted particular attention because instructors turn the music up.

qs.q: The share of younger patients at one clinic has risen over an audiologist’s career.
qs.ev: roughly one in five new patients is under forty, compared with almost none when she started her career
qs.x: Paragraph A: one in five new patients is now under forty, compared with almost none when Pruitt began.

qs.q: Canada plans to introduce sound limits for concert venues within the next two years.
qs.x: Paragraph C says Canada has no national standard for venues, but no future plan or timeline is mentioned.

qs.q: A hearing test may be paid for by an employer’s plan even if the province does not cover it.
qs.ev: many workplace benefit plans pay for it
qs.x: Paragraph D: basic tests are not publicly covered in most provinces, but many workplace benefit plans pay.

p4.title: It’s Time to Check ID for Energy Drinks
p4.byline: Opinion | by Garrett Lunn, high school vice-principal
p4.text:
Every morning, I watch students arrive at our school carrying cans the size of a small flower vase. They are not drinking coffee; most teenagers find coffee too bitter. They are drinking energy drinks – brightly coloured, heavily sweetened and packed with caffeine. A single large can may contain more than three hundred milligrams of caffeine, nearly three times what health authorities suggest as a daily maximum for a fifteen-year-old.

I am not a doctor, and I will not pretend to be one. But I have spent twenty years in high schools, and I know what I see. I see students who cannot sit still in first period and who crash by lunch. I see students who stay up until two in the morning gaming, sleep for four hours, and then drink two cans to get through the day, a cycle that repeats until something breaks. Last year, two of our students were taken to hospital with racing hearts after drinking several cans before a basketball tournament. Both recovered, thankfully. Neither knew how much caffeine they had consumed.

That is why I believe the province should ban the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to anyone under eighteen, as several European countries have done. Stores already check identification for lottery tickets and cigarettes. Adding one more product to that list is hardly a burden.

The usual objection is that a ban is heavy-handed, and that parents, not governments, should decide what their children drink. I have some sympathy for that argument. I am a parent myself, and I do not enjoy being told how to raise my children. But the reality is that most of these purchases happen when parents are nowhere near: at the convenience store across from the school, at the gas station on the way to practice. A parent cannot supervise a fifteen-year-old with twenty dollars and a bus pass.

Others argue that teenagers will simply get the drinks from older friends, or switch to coffee. Some will, no doubt. Bans are never perfect. Yet age limits on tobacco did not stop every teenager from smoking, and nobody seriously argues that they should be abolished. What they did was make smoking less convenient and less normal, and youth smoking rates fell dramatically. I expect the same would happen here.

It is also worth noting what a ban would not do. It would not prevent adults from buying energy drinks, and it would not cover coffee, tea or soft drinks with modest caffeine levels. The rule should target drinks above a clear threshold – say, eighty milligrams per serving – so that it is simple to enforce.

Finally, I would like to see the beverage companies take some responsibility. Their marketing is unmistakably aimed at young people: sponsorships of gaming tournaments and extreme sports, and social media influencers who are barely older than my students. Restricting that advertising should be part of any serious plan.

Schools can do their part. We have removed energy drinks from our cafeteria, and we talk about caffeine in health class. But we cannot control what happens across the street, and we should not have to fight this battle alone. That requires a law.

qs.q: What does the writer say about his qualifications to discuss this issue?
o: He has studied the medical research closely.
He has worked with doctors at his school.
He is speaking mainly as a worried parent.
He relies on what he has seen at work.
qs.ev: I have spent twenty years in high schools, and I know what I see.
qs.x: He admits he is not a doctor and bases his view on twenty years of observing students. He mentions being a parent only when discussing the parental-choice objection.

qs.q: Why does the writer mention the basketball tournament?
o: To show that athletes need more caffeine
To argue that sports events should be cancelled
To show students underestimate what they consume
To prove that energy drinks are often fatal
qs.ev: Neither knew how much caffeine they had consumed.
qs.x: The students ended up in hospital without knowing how much caffeine they had taken. Both recovered, so the story does not show the drinks are often fatal.

qs.q: What is the writer’s attitude toward the argument that parents should decide?
o: He partly agrees but finds it unrealistic.
He rejects it as completely unreasonable.
He accepts it and changes his proposal.
He thinks it applies only to young children.
qs.ev: I have some sympathy for that argument.
qs.x: He has “some sympathy” as a parent but argues parents can’t supervise purchases near school. He does not dismiss it completely, nor does he change his proposal.

qs.q: Why does the writer compare energy drinks to tobacco?
o: To show that both cause heart problems
To show an imperfect rule can still work
To argue for higher taxes on both
To show teens prefer energy drinks
qs.ev: Bans are never perfect.
qs.x: Tobacco age limits didn’t stop every teen but still cut youth smoking, so an imperfect ban can work. Taxes are never mentioned.

qs.q: What does the writer propose about which drinks a ban should cover?
o: It should include coffee sold to teenagers.
It should apply to every drink with caffeine.
It should be based on a set caffeine level.
It should be decided by each school board.
qs.ev: The rule should target drinks above a clear threshold
qs.x: He suggests a clear threshold, such as eighty milligrams per serving. He explicitly excludes coffee, tea and low-caffeine soft drinks.

comment.intro: Here is a comment posted by a reader in response to the article. Complete the comment by choosing the best option for each blank.
comment.text:
I run a convenience store two blocks from a high school, so I read this with interest. I’ll admit the writer is right that {1}. I see the same kids in my store every morning before the bell, and I’ve noticed the cans getting bigger every year.

But I don’t agree that checking ID would be {2}. Lottery tickets are kept behind the counter. Energy drinks sit in an open fridge next to the juice, and asking every teenager for ID at 8 a.m. with a line of customers is a recipe for arguments. If the province passes this law, it should also {3}, or small stores like mine will be left to deal with the fallout alone.

I also think he is too quick to dismiss the idea that {4}. Half my regulars would just send an eighteen-year-old in for them.

Where I fully agree with him is on {5}. The companies send me posters of gamers and skateboarders every month, and I stopped putting them up years ago.

o: teenagers find coffee too bitter
most buying happens out of parents’ sight
schools have removed the drinks from cafeterias
youth smoking fell after age limits
blanks.ev: most of these purchases happen when parents are nowhere near
blanks.x: The store owner confirms he sees students buying before school, supporting the writer’s point that purchases happen away from parents. The other options are mentioned in the article but don’t match his evidence.

o: simple to enforce
heavy-handed
a parent’s job
hardly a burden
blanks.ev: Adding one more product to that list is hardly a burden.
blanks.x: The commenter contrasts lottery tickets with energy drinks to challenge the writer’s claim that ID checks are “hardly a burden”. “Simple to enforce” refers to the caffeine threshold, not ID checks.

o: ban energy drinks for adults too
pay for health classes in schools
give stores support to enforce it
remove coffee from school cafeterias
blanks.ev: asking every teenager for ID at 8 a.m. with a line of customers is a recipe for arguments
blanks.x: His worry is that small stores would struggle to enforce the rule alone, so he wants support for retailers. Banning sales to adults is something the writer explicitly does not propose.

o: teens will get older friends to buy for them
parents should make these decisions
energy drinks are less harmful than coffee
advertising has little effect on teenagers
blanks.ev: Others argue that teenagers will simply get the drinks from older friends
blanks.x: His example of regulars sending an eighteen-year-old shows he takes the “older friends” objection more seriously than the writer, who answers it with “Some will, no doubt.”

o: removing drinks from cafeterias
limiting how the drinks are marketed
teaching about caffeine in class
the eighty-milligram threshold
blanks.ev: Restricting that advertising should be part of any serious plan.
blanks.x: His refusal to display posters of gamers and skateboarders matches the writer’s call to restrict marketing aimed at young people. Cafeterias and classes are school measures he does not discuss.

t1.situation: Last weekend, you took part in a 10-kilometre charity run in your city. Several things went wrong during the event. Write an email to the event organizer.
bullets: Explain why you took part in the event
Suggest improvements for next year’s event
t1.model:
Dear Ms. Okonkwo,

I took part in last Sunday’s Run for Hope 10K, and I am writing to share some feedback. I registered because my aunt is being treated at the cancer centre the run supports, and my whole family ran in her honour wearing matching shirts.

Unfortunately, several problems spoiled the day. The race started almost forty minutes late with no announcement explaining the delay, so hundreds of runners stood shivering in the parking lot. More seriously, the water station at the five-kilometre mark had run out of cups by the time the middle of the pack arrived. It was a humid morning, and I saw at least two runners who looked close to fainting. Finally, a missing sign near the river path sent several of us nearly a kilometre in the wrong direction.

For next year, I would suggest doubling the supplies at each water station, placing a volunteer at every turn, and texting participants if the schedule changes.

The cause is truly worthwhile, and I would happily run again. I hope these suggestions are helpful.

Kind regards,
Rhys Mercer

t2.intro: Your city has money for one new health and fitness project and is asking residents which project it should fund.
t2.question: Which option do you prefer? Explain the reasons for your choice.
t2.a: Option A: An outdoor fitness park with free exercise equipment, a running track and lighting for evening use, built in the city’s largest park.
t2.b: Option B: Free swimming lessons for every child aged 5 to 12 in the city, offered at existing pools for the next three years.
t2.model:
I would choose Option A, the outdoor fitness park, because it would serve every age group for decades rather than one group for a few years.

Free swimming lessons are a wonderful idea, and I fully understand why parents would support them. Learning to swim can save lives, especially in a country with so many lakes. However, the program would end after three years, and many families already pay for lessons through schools or community centres. Once the funding ran out, there would be nothing left to show for it.

A fitness park, by contrast, is a permanent investment. Teenagers could use the track after school, seniors could use the gentler equipment in the mornings, and shift workers could exercise in the evenings thanks to the lighting. Most importantly, it would be completely free, which matters for people who cannot afford a gym. I would use it myself, since my nearest gym costs sixty dollars a month.

Of course, the city would need to maintain the equipment and keep the park safe at night. Even so, a facility that everyone can use, every day, seems like the better use of public money.

t1.prompt: Your friend has recently started working night shifts at a hospital and is having trouble sleeping during the day. They feel exhausted all the time. Give your friend some advice.
t1.model: Oh, I really feel for you. Night shifts are brutal, and it’s no surprise you’re exhausted, because your body is basically fighting the sun. Here are a few things that might help. First, make your bedroom as dark as a cave. Get blackout curtains, or even tape cardboard over the window for now, and wear an eye mask. Light is the biggest signal that tells your brain to wake up. Second, protect your sleep like it’s an appointment. Put your phone on do-not-disturb, and tell your roommates that your sleeping hours are off-limits unless it’s an emergency. Earplugs or a fan for white noise can help with daytime noise too. Third, be careful with caffeine. I know it’s tempting to drink coffee all night, but try not to have any in the last four or five hours of your shift, or you’ll be lying in bed wide awake. Also, wear sunglasses on the drive home, so the morning light doesn’t wake you up completely. Finally, try to keep a similar schedule on your days off, at least partly. And if things don’t improve in a month or so, talk to your doctor, because constant exhaustion isn’t something to ignore.

t2.prompt: Talk about a time when you tried a new sport or physical activity for the first time. What was it, and how did it go?
t2.model: Last winter, a coworker convinced me to try cross-country skiing. I’d only done downhill skiing as a kid, so I assumed it would be easy. I was very wrong. We went to a trail just outside the city on a Saturday morning, and within ten minutes I’d fallen three times, mostly because the skis are so narrow and the boots don’t support your ankles at all. Going uphill was the worst part. I kept sliding backwards while seniors in their seventies glided past me, smiling. But after about an hour, something clicked. I figured out the rhythm, and on the flat parts it actually felt like flying. By the end, I was soaked in sweat even though it was minus fifteen. I was incredibly sore the next day, but I loved it, and a month later I bought a used set of skis.

scene.alt: A bright community kitchen during a healthy cooking class. On the back wall there is a whiteboard that says “HEALTHY MEALS 101”, a round clock and a large window. Behind a long grey counter on the left, an instructor with dark skin, wearing a white shirt and a white chef’s hat with her hair in a bun, points toward the class, and next to her a man in a purple shirt holds up a tray. A green box labelled “VEG” sits on the counter. In the front on the right, around a wooden table with a red mug on it, a woman with long hair in an orange top reads a recipe book, an older man with grey hair and glasses holds a cup, and a young boy in a green shirt carries a tray of red tomatoes. There is a potted plant in the corner.

t3.prompt: Describe some things that are happening in the picture as well as you can. The person you are speaking to cannot see the picture.
t3.model: This looks like a cooking class in a bright community kitchen. On the back wall, there’s a whiteboard that says “Healthy Meals 101”, so I think they’re learning to make nutritious, affordable food. There’s also a round clock and a big window. On the left, behind a long grey counter, the instructor is wearing a white shirt and a chef’s hat, and she’s pointing toward the class as if she’s explaining the next step. Beside her, a man in a purple shirt is holding up a tray, and there’s a green box of vegetables on the counter. On the right, a few participants are gathered around a wooden table. A woman with long hair is reading a recipe book, an older man with glasses is holding a cup, maybe tasting something, and a little boy is carrying a tray of red tomatoes.

t4.prompt: In this picture, what do you think will most probably happen next?
t4.model: I think the instructor is about to call everyone over to the counter for a demonstration. She’s pointing at the group, so she’s probably saying something like, “Okay, bring your tomatoes over here.” The little boy will carry his tray of tomatoes to the counter, and the instructor will probably show him how to chop them safely, maybe for a fresh salsa or a vegetable soup. The man in purple will set his tray down, and they’ll start pulling vegetables out of the green box. The woman with the recipe book will most likely read out the ingredients so everyone can follow along. As for the older man with the cup, I imagine he’ll finish his drink and join in, too. By the end of the class, they’ll all sit around the table and taste what they’ve made, and hopefully take the recipe home.

t5.intro: Your 10-year-old child wants to try a new after-school activity. You have found two options. Choose the option that you prefer. In the next section, you will need to persuade a family member that your choice is better than the one they prefer.
t5.persuade: Your partner prefers the hip-hop dance class. Persuade your partner that your choice is better.
t5.model: I know Maya loves dancing, and a stage show would be exciting, but I really think karate is the better fit right now. First, the dance class is mostly kids aged eleven to thirteen. Maya’s only ten, and she’s pretty shy, so being the youngest in a group of almost-teenagers could make her want to quit. At karate, groups are organized by belt, not age. Second, think about logistics. Karate is walking distance from school, so she can go straight there. The dance studio is a thirty-minute bus ride downtown, which means one of us gives up every Saturday morning. Third, karate is twice a week, so she’d get more exercise, and the belt tests give her goals to work toward. Yes, it costs a bit more with the uniform, but I think it’s worth it.

t6.situation: You share a small office with a coworker who often comes to work while sick, coughing and sneezing all day. Your partner is going through cancer treatment, and the doctor has warned that even a minor infection could be serious. Your coworker has told you they cannot afford to take unpaid sick days.
options: Talk to your coworker and explain your concern.
Talk to your supervisor and ask for a change to the office arrangements.
t6.note: Choose ONE option and speak to that person.
t6.model: Hey Ben, do you have a minute? I wanted to talk to you privately, and I hope you won’t take it the wrong way. I know you’ve been feeling under the weather this week, and I really get that taking unpaid days isn’t easy. The thing is, my wife is in the middle of chemotherapy, and her doctor told us that even a bad cold could put her in hospital. So I’m being extra careful about what I bring home. Would you be okay with a couple of things? Maybe wearing a mask on days when you’re coughing, and I could move my laptop to the empty desk by the window so there’s more space between us. Also, our team can work from home two days a week, so on days you feel sick, that might be an option without losing pay. Thanks for understanding.

t7.prompt: Some people think advertising for junk food and sugary drinks aimed at children should be banned, including on television, websites and social media. Others think parents, not governments, should control what children eat. What is your opinion? Explain your reasons.
t7.model: I believe junk food advertising aimed at children should be banned, and I have two main reasons. First, children simply can’t understand advertising the way adults can. A seven-year-old who sees a cartoon character selling sugary cereal doesn’t realize that a company is trying to persuade them. They just see something fun and colourful, and then they beg their parents for it in the grocery store. That isn’t a fair fight, and it puts a lot of pressure on parents. Second, childhood obesity rates have risen a lot over the last few decades, and the habits kids form early tend to stay with them for life. Advertising isn’t the only cause, of course, but it’s one we can actually control. Some countries already have rules like this, and their advertising industries didn’t collapse. Now, I understand the argument that parents should be in charge, and I agree that parents have the main responsibility. But today, kids see ads on tablets and phones when parents aren’t even in the room, so it’s unrealistic to expect them to filter everything. A ban wouldn’t stop anyone from buying a chocolate bar. It would just stop companies from targeting kids directly.

scene.alt: A street with an unusual building shaped like a giant white coffee mug, about as tall as a two-storey house, with a huge curved handle on its right side. A green door has been cut into the front of the mug, and there is a small square window above the door. A “FOR RENT” sign stands on the sidewalk to the left, where a man in a red shirt is pointing at the building. On the right, a woman in a dark blue dress holds a takeaway cup and looks at the mug, next to a streetlamp and a purple bicycle. Two small potted plants sit beside the entrance, and there is a sun and a cloud in the sky.

t8.prompt: You and a friend are planning to open a smoothie and juice bar, and you have found this unusual building for rent. Call your friend, describe the building, and explain whether you think it would be a good place for your business. Your friend cannot see the picture.
t8.model: Hey Tasha, you have to hear about this place I just found on Elm Street. The whole building is shaped like a giant white coffee mug. I’m not kidding. It’s about two storeys tall, perfectly round, and there’s a huge curved handle sticking out of the right side. Someone cut a green door into the front of the mug, and there’s a little square window above it. There are two potted plants by the entrance and a “For Rent” sign out front. People walking by keep stopping to point at it and take photos. Honestly, I think it could be perfect for us. It’s impossible to miss, so we’d get free advertising every day. The only problem is the image – it looks like a coffee shop, not a juice bar. But we could paint it bright green and call it something like “The Big Cup”. Want to see it tomorrow?
